title: Delete Columns to Make Sorted III
statement:
The strings in `strs` all have the same length, so stack them as the rows of a grid whose columns are character positions. Deleting a column removes the character at that position from every string at once, and you may delete any set of columns.

Return the fewest columns you must delete so that every remaining string is sorted on its own: reading it left to right, no character is greater than the one after it. The rows do not need to be in order relative to each other.
constraints: All strings in strs have the same length
strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Minimising deleted columns is the same as maximising kept columns. A set of kept columns works exactly when, for every pair of consecutive kept columns `i < j`, each row has `row[i] <= row[j]`. So treat each column as an item and say column `i` "fits before" column `j` when that holds in every row: the task becomes a longest non-decreasing subsequence over columns. Trying every subset of columns also works, but costs O(2^m).

## Approach

1. Let `cols` be the string length and give every column `dp[j] = 1` (a chain of just itself).
2. For each column `j`, look at every earlier column `i`.
3. Scan all rows; `fits` stays true only if no row has `row[i] > row[j]`.
4. If `i` fits before `j`, extend the best chain ending at `i`: `dp[j] = max(dp[j], dp[i] + 1)`.
5. Track the largest chain in `longest` and return `cols - longest`.

## Example 1, step by step

`strs = ["babca", "bbazb"]`, so the columns read `(b,b) (a,b) (b,a) (c,z) (a,b)`.

- `j = 1`: column 0 has `b > a` in row 0, so `dp[1] = 1`.
- `j = 2`: both earlier columns have a `b` above the `a` in row 1, so `dp[2] = 1`.
- `j = 3`: `(c,z)` is at least as large as every earlier column in both rows, so `dp[3] = 2`.
- `j = 4`: only column 1 `(a,b)` fits before `(a,b)`, so `dp[4] = 2`.

`longest = 2`, so the answer is `5 - 2 = 3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m² · n): each of the m² column pairs is checked against all n rows.
- Space: O(m) for `dp`.

## Pitfalls

- A pair of columns must agree in **every** row; checking only the first row gives too small an answer.
- Use `>` to reject, so equal characters are allowed (rows need only be non-decreasing).
- Start `longest` at 1, not 0: a single column is always sorted, so with one column the answer is 0.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cols` | number of columns (the common string length) |
| `dp[j]` | most columns that can be kept when column `j` is the last one kept |
| `longest` | largest `dp` value seen so far |
| `i`, `j` | earlier candidate column and current column |
| `fits` | whether column `i` may sit right before column `j` in every row |
| `row` | one string of `strs` |

narration.2: Every string has the same length, so this is the number of columns.
narration.3: On its own, every column is a sorted chain of length 1.
narration.4: The best chain so far keeps at least one column.
narration.5: Treat column j as the last column kept in a chain.
narration.6: Try every earlier column i as the one kept just before j.
narration.8: Column i may precede column j only if every row agrees.
narration.9: This row would go down from column i to column j...
narration.10: ...so column i cannot sit right before column j.
narration.14: If i fits before j, the chain ending at i grows by one column.
narration.15: Record the longer chain ending at column j.
narration.18: Remember the longest chain of kept columns found so far.
narration.20: Every column outside the longest chain must be deleted.
